extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of classical geometry; readers of Archimedes (mathematics historians and geometers)
extracted.subtask_description: Geometric constructions and existence conditions for cutting spheres (by planes) to obtain segments with given volumetric or surface ratios, and related results (use of cones and conics, analysis/synthesis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent spherical segments by cones (Prop. 2 principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A spherical segment (cut off by a plane perpendicular to a diameter) is equal in volume to a cone having the same base circle and with apex on the axis (produced) chosen so that cone height relates appropriately to the segment's height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the propositions the method is to take points H (on OA produced) and H' (on OA' produced) so that cones HBB', H'BB' are respectively equal to the spherical segments BAB', BA'B'. Use that equality to translate problems about spherical segments into problems about cones (volumes reduce to heights of cones). See repeated uses in Props. 4–9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce volume-ratio problems to ratios of cone heights
rubrics_metrics.description: When a plane perpendicular to a diameter AA' cuts the sphere in BB' (bisected at right angles by AA' at M), the ratio of the volumes of the two segments equals the ratio of the heights of the corresponding cones (HM : H'M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus a target volume ratio can be enforced by constructing H and H' so that HM : H'M equals the given ratio; this reduces the 3-point problem (M, H, H') to algebraic/proportional equations to be solved for M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis and synthesis method (assume solution then construct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve by analysis: suppose the required plane (or point M) is found, derive algebraic proportional relations among constructed points; then in synthesis reconstruct those constructions reversing the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes explicitly carries out 'analysis' (derive relations under the assumption of a solution) and then 'synthesis' (give construction). The synthetic construction follows the algebraic equalities obtained in the analysis and uses auxiliary constructions (producing OA to D, dividing AD, constructing conics, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of auxiliary points via invariant ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: If three unknown points (M, H, H') appear in relations, find expressions for ratios A'H':H'M and HH':H'A' independent of H and H', then equate compound ratios to eliminate H,H' and obtain an equation in M alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes shows how to compute A'H':H'M and HH':H'A' from earlier proportional equations, then compounds them to match the known HH':H'M, thereby obtaining the determining relation for M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct OA-produced point D with OA = AD as a convenient symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: In many syntheses produce OA to D so that OA = AD; D then provides a symmetric segment AD which simplifies expressing ratios and constructing the desired division of AA'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice makes AD a given point from which AD:DE can be set equal to ratios derived from the problem; used repeatedly (e.g., in Prop. 4 synthesis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conics (parabola, rectangular hyperbola, ellipse) to locate intersection point determining M
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce certain cubic or higher relations to the intersection of a parabola with a rectangular hyperbola (or ellipse with hyperbola); the intersection point P yields lines/ordinates that determine M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete constructions: describe a parabola with given vertex, axis and parameter (constructed from earlier parallels/rectangles); describe a rectangular hyperbola with given asymptotes passing through a given point. Their intersection P (which is 'given in position') determines M by drawing through P a line parallel to a given direction. This approach is used to solve the subsidiary problem (division of AB) and to analyze the number of positive solutions of the resulting cubic (0,1,2 intersections correspond to 0/1/2 positive roots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence condition (διορισμός): analyze limits of possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Before synthesis, investigate necessary (and sometimes sufficient) inequalities that must hold for a solution to exist (e.g., constraints on products or ranges of parameters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in the subsidiary problem (divide AB at M so AM·MB^2 = AC·D) Archimedes shows a necessary condition that AC·D must not exceed a certain maximal value (computed geometrically), and describes when there are two solutions. Similarly, for the cone/segment ratio problem a necessary condition is that the given ratio be greater than 3:2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum principle for quadratic/cubic expressions via geometric extremum
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the maximal value of expressions like AM·MB^2 occurs at particular geometric configurations (e.g., when BM = 2AM), yielding necessary inequalities for solvability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the proof of impossibility/possibility of the auxiliary division problem; gives criterion for whether AC·D is within allowable bounds (compare to AO·OB^2 etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct P by building parallelograms and using rectangle equalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use constructions of parallels and parallelograms so that products/rectangles arising in algebraic relations correspond to geometric rectangles whose equality/localization give points like P and Q lying on given conics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: draw HBN through B parallel to AC meeting CM in N, construct parallelogram CENF, then measure HL along EN so that GH:TS = AB : (D) which leads to rectangles equalities used to derive that P lies on a given parabola/hyperbola.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate algebraic relations into conic defining properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert relations like PN^2 = EL·EN or GM·ME = AB·BE into the defining metric properties of a parabola or hyperbola respectively, so that points satisfying the algebraic relations are intersections of the constructed conics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the key step in passing from analytic relations to geometrical construction: match LHS product/square relations to standard conic properties (parabola: square of ordinate equals rectangle formed by parameter and abscissa; hyperbola: rectangle equality relating distances to asymptotes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean proportionals for similarity-and-volume constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: To construct a spherical segment similar to one and equal in volume to another, insert two mean proportionals between specified lengths (continued proportion) so that the resulting base diameter ef and other mean S produce the required similarity and volume equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes reduces the problem to finding ef, S in continued proportion between BB' and R (where R encodes a given ratio); then uses ef as diameter to build the required segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve similarity by matching corresponding diameters/ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing a segment similar to a given segment, set the new segment's diameter d'd so that d'd : AB = D'D : DF (from similarity), which makes d'd a given length and hence fixes the required construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in the synthesis of the construction for a segment similar to DEF and having surface equal to ABB' (Prop. 6): determine d'd from similarity relations, then cut and erect the plane perpendicular to d'd to obtain def.

rubrics_metrics.name: Given ratio-to-cone problem: ensure given ratio exceeds 3:2
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked for a segment whose volume has a given ratio to the cone with same base and equal height, a necessary condition is that the given ratio must be greater than 3:2; otherwise no solution exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes derives that OA'+A'M : A'M must equal the given ratio, and shows via inequalities that OA'+A'M : A'M > 3:2 is necessary for a construction to be possible. In synthesis one picks DE:EF equal to the given ratio (greater than 3:2) and finds M accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequalities relating segment volumes and surfaces (Prop. 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sphere is cut into two segments (A'BB' greater, ABB' lesser), then (segment volumes) : (segment volumes) < (surfaces of segments)^2 : (other surface)^2 but > (surfaces) : (other surface)^1.5 — expressed as: greater_segment : lesser_segment is less than the duplicate of the ratio of their surfaces, but greater than the sesquialterate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes proves inequalities comparing volumes and areas by constructing cones equal to segments and comparing heights and diameters; these inequalities provide ordering relations useful in extremal arguments (e.g., hemisphere maximizes volume among segments with equal surface).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hemisphere maximizes volume among segments with equal surface (Prop. 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all spherical segments having equal surface area, the hemisphere has the greatest volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by comparing cones equal to segments and hemispheres and using algebraic inequalities on diameters and heights; practical criterion: to maximize volume for fixed surface, aim for the hemisphere configuration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a circle equals right triangle (radius × circumference) (Measurement Prop.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of any circle is equal to a right-angled triangle in which one side about the right angle equals the radius and the other equals the circumference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes proves by exhaustion: inscribe polygons (to contradict 'circle area greater than triangle') and circumscribe polygons (to contradict 'less than triangle'), using successive bisections to make polygonal approximations arbitrarily close.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound circumference by perimeters of inscribed/circumscribed polygons (Pi bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate the circumference by perimeters of regular inscribed and circumscribed polygons (e.g., 96-sided) to obtain bounds for the ratio circumference:diameter — specifically less than 31/7 and greater than 223/71 in Archimedes' proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: repeatedly bisect angles to increase polygon sides, use trigonometric/Euclidean computations of chord/tangent lengths (via angle bisections) to bound OA:AG etc., and hence perimeter. This yields the classical bounds 223/71 < C/D < 22/7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction via polygon approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove equality claims about circle area, assume area greater (or less) than reference triangle, then inscribe (or circumscribe) polygons with sufficiently many sides so that their area contradicts that assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct polygons whose area is respectively larger or smaller than the assumed 'excess' and use properties: perpendicular from centre to polygon side equals radius for inscribed case, perimeter comparisons for circumscribed case, to derive contradiction.
